title: Designing a Concurrent Data Structure's Contract
summary: Specifying what a concurrent class actually promises callers under simultaneous access -- linearizability, atomic compound operations, and the difference between a contract and an implementation detail.

slides.markdown:
"Thread-safe" is not a contract by itself -- it doesn't say what a caller can actually assume about ordering, atomicity of compound calls, or what one thread is guaranteed to see after another thread's write. This topic is about writing that contract down precisely, the way a well-documented concurrent library does.

Think of it like a restaurant order guarantee: "we won't lose your order" (thread-safe, doesn't crash) is very different from "orders are served in the exact sequence they were placed" (a specific ordering guarantee). Most concurrency bugs at this level come from a caller assuming the stronger promise when only the weaker one was ever made.

Saying a class is "thread-safe" only promises one thing: it won't corrupt its internal state or crash under concurrent access. It says nothing about **ordering** (if Thread A's write happens before Thread B's read starts, is B guaranteed to see it?), nothing about **atomicity of multi-step operations** (is check-then-act safe?), and nothing about what happens during a **partial failure** mid-operation.

Two classes can both be honestly labeled "thread-safe" while making very different promises: one might guarantee every reader sees the most recent write immediately (strong consistency); another might let readers see a slightly stale value for a while (eventual consistency) in exchange for higher throughput. Both are correctly "thread-safe" -- they just made different contracts.

This is why, at the expert level, "is it thread-safe?" is the wrong question. The right one is "which specific guarantees does it make, and do those match what my code assumes?" -- getting a class to [designing-thread-safe-classes](designing-thread-safe-classes) gets you to correctness; this topic gets you to a precise, documented contract.

**Linearizability** is the strongest common ordering guarantee for a concurrent object: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some single point between when it was called and when it returned, and all threads agree on that same global order. In practice this means: once a `put(k, v)` call returns, every subsequent `get(k)` from any thread -- no matter which core or CPU cache it runs on -- sees `v`, not a stale prior value.

**Happens-before** is the underlying relationship that makes ordering guarantees precise: if operation X happens-before operation Y, every thread is guaranteed to see the effects of X once it observes Y. A lock's release happens-before the next thread's acquire of that same lock -- that's specifically why locks provide visibility, not just mutual exclusion.

Without an explicit happens-before relationship, a thread has no guarantee it will ever see another thread's write, even long after it happened -- the writing CPU core's cache may simply not have propagated it yet. This is why "just remove the lock, it slowed us down" can silently break correctness even without changing what any single thread computes.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: what the contract guarantees under a race
slides.markdown:
![Thread A's put completes before Thread B's get begins, so B is guaranteed to see A's value](assets/linearizability-timeline.svg)

Thread A calls `put("k", 1)`. Thread B calls `get("k")` at roughly the same time -- the contract's answer depends entirely on the ordering. If B's `get` call starts strictly *after* A's `put` call has already returned, a linearizable map guarantees B sees `1`. If the calls genuinely overlap in time, the map is free to return either the old or new value -- both are valid outcomes because the ordering between overlapping calls isn't defined.

The diagram is the answer to "what am I actually promised here?" -- and it's specifically not "always the latest value," it's "the latest value once there's a completed operation to be after."

assets.alt: Thread A's put completes before Thread B's get begins, so B is guaranteed to see A's value

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: check-then-act needs the contract to say it's atomic
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'm using a thread-safe concurrent map, so `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` is safe."

**Why it's wrong:** the map's contract guarantees each individual call -- `containsKey`, `put` -- is safe. It says nothing about a *sequence* of two calls being atomic together, because that's a stronger, separate guarantee the contract has to explicitly offer. Two threads can both call `containsKey(k)`, both see `false`, and both proceed to `put(k, v)` -- exactly the race from earlier in this group, still alive even on a fully thread-safe map.

**Correct model:** check whether the specific compound operation you need is explicitly part of the contract -- `ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent(k, v)` documents that exact check-then-act as a single atomic operation. If the contract doesn't name your compound operation as atomic, assume it isn't, no matter how thread-safe the individual pieces are.

slides.subTitle: Java example

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: weak vs strong consistency guarantees
slides.markdown:
| | Strong consistency (linearizable) | Weak/eventual consistency |
|---|---|---|
| What a read after a write sees | Always the latest completed write, everywhere | Possibly a stale value for some window of time |
| Typical cost | More coordination -- can reduce throughput | Higher throughput, less coordination needed |
| Example | `synchronized` methods, most single-node `ConcurrentHashMap` operations | Iterators over `ConcurrentHashMap` (weakly consistent -- may or may not reflect concurrent modifications) |
| Best fit | Correctness-critical single values (a lock's own state, a counter) | High-throughput reads where slightly stale data is acceptable (a metrics snapshot, a cache) |

**How to decide:** ask what actually breaks if a reader sees a value that's a few milliseconds stale. If nothing breaks, weak consistency buys real throughput for free; if a stale read causes a wrong decision (double-charging, double-booking), you need the stronger guarantee even at a coordination cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Contract vs implementation detail: what to document
slides.markdown:
A concurrent class's documentation should state exactly three things as its **contract**: what ordering guarantee it makes (linearizable, or weaker -- and where), which compound operations are atomic by name (`putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, not just the primitives), and what a caller can assume during iteration or bulk operations while another thread is mutating.

Everything else -- whether it uses one lock or sixteen, CAS or `synchronized`, a hash table or a skip list -- is an **implementation detail** that should be free to change without breaking any caller, precisely because callers never depended on it. `ConcurrentHashMap`'s internal locking strategy has changed across Java versions; its documented contract (its atomic methods, its weakly-consistent iterators) hasn't, which is exactly why nobody's code broke.

The discipline this teaches: when you design a concurrent class, write the contract section of the documentation *before* the implementation. If you can't state precisely what it guarantees, you don't yet know what you're building -- you're just writing code and hoping it's safe.
